summary: Help children aged 7–9 give each of the eight planets a vivid, memorable signature identity anchored to real photographs: Mercury smallest/closest, Venus hottest, Mars red (rust), Jupiter largest with the Great Red Spot, Saturn with bright rings, Uranus tipped on its side, Neptune farthest and bitterly cold. The aim is identity-building with light comparison ('Jupiter is far bigger than Earth'), one causal 'why' worth teaching (Mars's red = iron oxide/rust), and one counter-intuitive comparison worth surfacing (Venus, not closest Mercury, is hottest, because its thick atmosphere traps heat).
misconceptions: The closest planet to the Sun (Mercury) must be the hottest (Venus is hottest — its thick atmosphere traps heat)
Only Saturn has rings (all four gas giants have ring systems; Saturn's are just the brightest and most obvious)
Mars is red because it is hot / on fire (it is cold; the red is iron oxide — rust — in its rocks)
The Great Red Spot is a feature on the surface (Jupiter has no solid surface; the Spot is a giant long-lived storm in its atmosphere)
All planets are roughly Earth-like / you could stand on any of them (the gas giants have no solid surface; conditions range from scorching to freezing)

activities.title: Visit Eight Very Different Worlds
steps: Look at a real photograph of each planet alongside one bold signature fact: Saturn's bright rings, Jupiter's swirling Great Red Spot, Uranus lying on its side, tiny Mercury hugging the Sun, rusty-red Mars, bitterly cold Neptune farthest out.

For Mars, first say what you think 'red' might mean, then reveal: a close-up of rusty soil beside an old rusty nail — 'Mars is red for the same reason old iron goes orange: rust (iron oxide) in its rocks.'
For the 'which planet is hottest?' question, make a prediction before revealing the answer: it is Venus, not Mercury, because Venus is wrapped in a thick blanket of air that traps the Sun's heat.
Link each planet back to its place in the order of the eight planets.
activities.insight: Each planet is a genuinely distinct world with its own striking feature; and a planet's temperature depends on more than its distance from the Sun — its atmosphere matters too.

activities.title: Match the Feature to the Right Planet
steps: Match each feature to its planet: rings → Saturn, Great Red Spot → Jupiter, red/rust → Mars, tilted on its side → Uranus, smallest and closest → Mercury, hottest → Venus, farthest and very cold → Neptune.
Answer: 'Which planet is the hottest?' — choosing from options that include the tempting Mercury (closest) distractor.
Answer: 'Why is Mars red?' — choosing rust/iron oxide rather than heat or fire.
State one distinctive feature for at least six of the eight planets in your own words.
activities.insight: Distinctive features stay attached to the correct planet rather than blurring into a single list of names.

activities.title: Order and Build the Fact Files
steps: Drag or place the planets into order from hottest to coldest by typical (average) temperature, accepting Uranus and Neptune in either order as the two coldest, then from smallest to largest, and talk through the ordering using 'bigger/hotter/colder than'.
Assemble each planet's fact card from feature tiles (image + signature feature + one comparison).
Say at least one comparison aloud, e.g. 'Jupiter is much bigger than Earth' or 'Venus is hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer.'
activities.insight: Planets can be compared along size and temperature, and ordering them makes the surprising cases (Venus hotter than closer Mercury) stand out.

activities.title: Explain the Puzzle: Why Is Venus Hotter?
steps: Respond to the prompt: 'Mercury is closest to the Sun, so you might expect it to be hottest. But Venus is hotter than Mercury. How can a planet that is further from the Sun end up hotter? Tell me WHY.'

Explain in your own words that Venus's thick atmosphere of gases traps the Sun's heat like a blanket and lets it escape only very slowly, while Mercury has almost no atmosphere so its heat leaks away.

Consider follow-up questions: What does a thick atmosphere do to the heat a planet gets? Which matters more for how hot a planet is — only distance, or atmosphere too? If Mars is red because of rust, does that tell us it is hot, or something else? Why can't Jupiter's Great Red Spot be a mark painted on the ground?
activities.insight: A planet's temperature is shaped by its atmosphere as well as its distance from the Sun; the 'closer = hotter' rule alone cannot explain Venus.

checkQuestion: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun, so you might expect it to be the hottest. But actually Venus is hotter than Mercury. How can a planet that is FURTHER from the Sun end up hotter? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: Venus is the hottest planet even though Mercury is closer to the Sun because Venus is wrapped in a very thick atmosphere of gases that traps the Sun's heat like a blanket and won't let it escape (a runaway greenhouse effect). Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its heat leaks away, especially at night. So distance from the Sun isn't the only thing that sets a planet's temperature — its atmosphere matters too. (Mars, by the way, looks red because its rocks and dust are full of iron oxide — rust.)
